checks.claim: Key: on a non-spinning Earth heated most at the equator, the wind near the ground blows from the poles toward the equator
checks.note: NOAA: without rotation 'global circulation would be simple': warm air rises at the equator, moves toward the poles aloft, and the cooled air returns 'south to the equator' near the ground.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Blow from the equator toward the poles' (that is the return flow high above, not the ground wind)
Wrong: 'Blow from west to east all round the world' (west-to-east needs the spin's deflection)
checks.note: Grokipedia: the Coriolis effect 'deflects poleward-moving meridional flows eastward' to make the westerlies; no spin, no deflection.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Barely blow, since the spin is what drives it' (uneven heating drives the wind; spin only bends it)
checks.note: Pressure gradients from heating drive the air; the Coriolis effect deflects but does not drive.

checks.claim: Context: heated air rises over the equator (low at the ground), cold air sinks at the poles (high), air flows from high to low
checks.note: Grokipedia: pressure gradient force accelerates air toward a low; convergence into a low 'causes it to rise'; highs have subsidence. NOAA: high-pressure band at about 30 N/S 'and at each pole'.

checks.claim: Stem: George Hadley was an English lawyer more interested in physics than law
checks.note: Called to the bar 1709 but 'remained more interested in mechanical and physical studies than in legal work'; Royal Society blog calls him a 'lawyer-turned-scientist' (https://royalsociety.org/blog/2015/07/debating-the-winds/); EBSCO: 'A barrister (lawyer) by training'.

checks.claim: Stem: Hadley explained the trade winds in 1735
checks.note: 'Concerning the cause of the general trade winds', Philosophical Transactions, 22 May 1735.

checks.claim: Stem: trade winds north of the equator blow from the northeast
checks.note: 'from the northeast in the Northern Hemisphere and from the southeast in the Southern Hemisphere'.

checks.claim: Key: Hadley said Earth's spin beneath the moving air turns them
checks.note: Grokipedia: Hadley tied the trades to 'differential solar heating combined with Earth's axial rotation'; the surface's eastward speed decreases poleward, so equatorward air lags westward.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'The air following the Sun's heat each day' (Halley's 1686 idea, not Hadley's)
checks.note: Halley: as Earth turned, 'the location of maximum heating from the Sun moved west across the Earth's surface' and the air followed; Hadley published a 'correction' to it (Royal Society blog).

checks.claim: Wrong: Moon's pull; ocean currents dragging the air
checks.note: Surface currents are 'driven primarily by wind friction on the surface', not the reverse; the Moon raises tides.

checks.claim: Context: Halley said in 1686 that the air follows the Sun's heat westward each day
checks.note: Royal Society: 'driving an easterly (westward) wind to follow on the path of most intense solar warming'. Presented 1685, published 1686 (An Historical Account of the Trade Winds, and Monsoons).

checks.claim: Context: 'Hadley was the first to bring in Earth's spin'
checks.note: Not true. Galileo, a century earlier, had already explained the trade winds by Earth's rotation: the air near the equator lagging behind the fast-spinning Earth (Wikipedia, Hadley cell; Irish Times, https://www.irishtimes.com/news/the-wherefore-of-the-wind-1.41140). EBSCO (https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/earth-and-atmospheric-sciences/hadley-describes-atmospheric-circulation): 'There was a consensus that these winds arose as the Earth rotated from west to east.' What Hadley added was how the spin turns air moving toward the equator, an element 'missing in Halley's proposal' (Wikipedia, George Hadley). Fix: replace 'Hadley was the first to bring in Earth's spin' with 'Hadley added what Halley had left out, the way Earth's spin turns air moving across it'.

checks.claim: Context: the circulation he described now bears his name
checks.note: Hadley cell / Hadley circulation.

checks.claim: Stem: Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis, a French engineer, in 1835 worked out motion on spinning machines such as water wheels
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'French mathematician and engineer' (1792-1843); 1835 'Memoire sur les equations du mouvement relatif des systemes de corps', relative motion in rotating machinery such as waterwheels. Wikipedia: 1835 paper 'on the energy yield of machines with rotating parts, such as waterwheels'.

checks.claim: Stem: weather scientists later used his mathematics for the winds
checks.note: 'Early in the 20th century, the term Coriolis force began to be used in connection with meteorology.'

checks.claim: Key: right in the Northern Hemisphere, left in the Southern
checks.note: Both Grokipedia and Wikipedia: right of the motion in the north, left in the south.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: left/right reversed; right in both; toward the east in both
Context: the bend fades to zero at the equator; equatorward winds on both sides end up easterly
checks.note: Horizontal deflection 'decreases to zero at the equator'.

checks.claim: Context: far too weak to steer a draining sink
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'the Coriolis effect is negligible at such small scales'; Wikipedia: 'repeatedly disproven'.

checks.claim: Stem: air sinks at about 30 N, building a high-pressure belt, and spreads both ways
checks.note: NOAA: 'The high pressure band is located at about 30 N/S latitude'; Grokipedia (Atmospheric circulation): 'sinking air at about 30 latitude creates subtropical high-pressure zones'.

checks.claim: Key: the poleward part becomes the westerlies
checks.note: Coriolis 'deflects poleward-moving meridional flows eastward'; NOAA: Ferrel cell surface air 'flows poleward and eastward'.

checks.claim: Context: from the southwest; belt about 30-60 degrees
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'approximately 30 and 60' degrees, southwest-to-northeast flow in the north (NOAA gives 35-60).

checks.claim: Wrong: polar easterlies (from polar highs, 60-90)
checks.note: Formed by 'outward divergence of cold, dense air' from polar highs, deflected to blow from the east.

checks.claim: Wrong: northeast trades (the equatorward part) and southeast trades (south of the equator)
Stem: Ooishi ran an observatory in Japan studying the upper air
checks.note: Director of the Tateno aerological observatory; Lewis (BAMS 2003) calls him its first director.

checks.claim: Stem: 1923 to 1925, more than a thousand balloons
checks.note: Grokipedia: 1923-1925, 'nearly 1,300 measurements' with pilot balloons; other counts 1,228 (Mar 1923-Feb 1925). 'More than a thousand' is safe.

checks.claim: Stem: balloons followed through a theodolite
checks.note: JMA: pilot balloon observation tracked 'a small hydrogen-filled balloon using an anemometric theodolite'; Tateno used the single-theodolite method from 1921.

checks.claim: Key: strong, steady winds from the west in winter
checks.note: Winter profile gave the first known evidence of 'persistent strong westerlies over Japan', later called the jet stream.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: easterlies; light winds dying away; light variable winds
Context: jet stream blows west to east, strongest in winter when temperature contrast is greatest
checks.note: 'predominantly flow from west to east'; polar jets 'intensifying ... in winter due to greater meridional temperature gradients'.

checks.claim: Context: published in Esperanto to reach abroad; little read outside Japan; found again in the 1930s
checks.note: Wikipedia (Oishi): Esperanto 'In an attempt to reach an unresponsive foreign audience'; Jet stream: 'largely went unnoticed outside Japan because it was published in Esperanto'; Wiley Post's 1930s high flights and Seilkopf's 'Strahlstromung' (1939).

checks.claim: Stem: B-29s over Japan late in 1944 met westerly winds up to about 320 km/h that scattered their bombs
checks.note: 24 Nov 1944: 'a high-speed wind coming out of the west at speeds as high as 200 miles per hour (320 km/h)', 'made accurate bombing impossible'; 3 Dec: jet stream 'scattering the bomb drops'. PBS confirms bombs overshot or fell short.

checks.claim: Key: storms below tend to travel along the jet's path
checks.note: 'the principal upper-level steering current for extratropical cyclones' and their fronts; Westerlies page: cyclones 'steered eastward along the axis of the westerly jet stream'.

checks.claim: Wrong: its winds drive the great ocean currents
checks.note: Surface currents are driven by wind friction at the sea surface, not by winds 9-16 km up.

checks.claim: Wrong: it shields the ground from ultraviolet light
checks.note: The ozone layer (about 15-35 km, mostly above the 9-16 km jets) absorbs UV.

checks.claim: Wrong: its path marks the hottest air
checks.note: Polar jets 'develop along the polar front, the boundary separating cold polar air masses from warmer mid-latitude air'.

checks.claim: Stem: WWI cut Norway off from Europe's weather reports
checks.note: 'the Germans cutting off Norway and the rest of Scandinavia from continental European weather communications'.

checks.claim: Stem: Vilhelm Bjerknes set up a dense web of stations across Norway
checks.note: Network expanded 'nearly tenfold'; Encyclopedia.com: 'a countrywide network of observation stations'; NASA: father and son 'established a network of weather observing stations in Norway'.

checks.claim: Stem: in Bergen, Vilhelm and Jacob named the lines 'fronts' after the war's battle fronts
checks.note: NASA: 'fronts', 'an analogy with the First World War battlefronts'; Grokipedia (Weather front) credits Vilhelm in 1918, Encyclopedia.com Jacob and colleagues in late 1919. The team also included Solberg and Bergeron; the stem does not say they worked alone.

checks.claim: Key: storms are born where cold polar air meets warm tropical air (the polar front)
checks.note: Polar front separates 'cold polar air masses from warmer tropical air masses'; Grokipedia (Bjerknes): 'Frontal waves - undulations along the polar front' grow into lows.

checks.claim: Wrong: damp sea air meets dry land air
checks.note: The Bergen front was a temperature boundary: 'cold air to the north' against 'warmer air to the south'.

checks.claim: Wrong: trades meet westerlies (they diverge from the 30-degree highs); northern and southern trades meet (at the ITCZ near the equator)
Stem: cold front brings towering thunderclouds, a short burst of heavy rain and gusts, then clearing and sharp cooling
checks.note: 'intense but short-lived showers, thunderstorms, gusty winds, and a sharp drop in temperature behind the front'.

checks.claim: Key: cold air pushes under the warm air and forces it up steeply
checks.note: UCAR: 'the heavier (more dense) cool air pushes under the lighter (less dense) warm air'; lifted warm air makes 'cumulus or cumulonimbus clouds and thunderstorms'.

checks.claim: Wrong: warm air pushes under cold air
checks.note: NWS: 'cold air is more dense (heavier) than warm air'.

checks.claim: Wrong: warm air climbs slowly up a long slope of cold air (that is a warm front)
Wrong: cold air sinks onto the warm air and squeezes out its rain
Stem: high thin cloud first, then a lower grey sheet, long steady rain, warmer air after
checks.note: Cirrus '500-1000 km ahead', ending in 'nimbostratus or stratus'; 'prolonged periods of light to moderate precipitation'; UCAR: warmer at the ground behind the front.

checks.claim: Key: warm air rides slowly up a gentle slope of cold air
checks.note: 'gentle slope due to the lower density of the warm air'; NWS: warm air flows 'upward in a slantwise manner over top low-level cool or cold air'.

checks.claim: Wrong: cold air shoves under warm air steeply (cold front); warm air rises straight up from sun-warmed ground (convection, not a front); cold air slides up over warm air (denser air does not ride over lighter)
Context: warm fronts move about half as fast as cold fronts
checks.note: UCAR: cold fronts move 'up to twice as fast as a warm front'; Grokipedia: warm 15-40 km/h against cold 40-48 km/h. 'About half' is a fair simplification.

checks.claim: Context: cold air never rides over warm air, being denser
checks.note: At a surface front the denser air stays low; even in a warm occlusion the overtaking air rides over colder air, not warmer. 'Never' is strong but true for a front at this level.

checks.claim: Key: a fast, steady barometer fall means a low moving in, with rising air and storms
checks.note: 'Falling pressure typically signals the approach of low-pressure systems associated with storms', 'rapid drops commonly preceding rain or thunderstorms'; Low-pressure area: convergence makes air rise, clouds and storms.

checks.claim: Wrong: a high moving in (rising pressure brings highs)
checks.note: 'rising pressure often precedes high-pressure systems bringing clear skies'.

checks.claim: Wrong: damp, heavy air settling (humid air is lighter than dry air)
checks.note: Water vapour about 18 g/mol against dry air about 29 g/mol, so 'any mixture of dry air and water vapor drops the weight of air'.

checks.claim: Wrong: cool, heavy air settling (that would raise the reading)
checks.note: Cold, dense air raises pressure; a fall means less air overhead.

checks.claim: Context: water vapour molecule lighter than the nitrogen and oxygen it replaces
checks.note: H2O 18 against N2 28 and O2 32.

checks.claim: Stem: tropics take in more solar energy than they give off over a year, polar regions the reverse
checks.note: 'a surplus of incoming solar radiation in tropical regions and a deficit in polar areas'; NASA Earth Observatory, Heating Imbalances (https://earthobservatory.nasa.gov/features/EnergyBalance/page3.php).

checks.claim: Key: winds and ocean currents carry heat toward the poles
checks.note: Ocean currents 'redistributing heat from tropics to poles', about 30-40 percent of the flux at 30 N; the atmosphere carries the rest (Grokipedia, Atmospheric circulation: about half).

checks.claim: Wrong: Earth's tilt shares out the sunlight evenly
checks.note: Annual mean insolation falls from about 400 W/m2 at the equator to about 150 W/m2 near 80 degrees; the poles get far less over a year.

checks.claim: Wrong / context: heat from Earth's interior is a few hundredths of a percent of absorbed sunlight
checks.note: 44-47 TW, about 0.09 W/m2, 'about 0.04% of the absorbed solar radiation (~240 W/m2)'. The core's own share (5-15 TW) is smaller still, so the 'core' wording only understates it.

checks.claim: Wrong / context: polar ice reflects most of the sunlight, rather than soaking it up
checks.note: Fresh snow 0.80-0.90, sea ice 0.50-0.70, open ocean about 0.06.

checks.claim: Context: a warm poleward current warms the air and gives its coast milder winters
checks.note: Warm currents moderate coastal winters (no named current is asked).

unit_notes: 10 ok, 1 error, 0 uncertain. The one error is in a context: fe1637f24b says Hadley 'was the first to bring in Earth's spin', but Galileo had explained the trade winds by Earth's rotation a century before; Hadley's first was showing how the spin turns air moving toward the equator, which Halley's theory lacked. Sources disagree on Ooishi's station (Grokipedia gives both 'Toya' and 'near Mount Fuji'; Wikipedia's Oishi page, Lewis in BAMS and the JMA give Tateno), on his balloon count (1,228 to about 1,300), and on the B-29 wind speeds (200 to 250 mph). The questions avoid all three, so nothing depends on them. Grokipedia's Hadley_cell page calls Hadley 'Secretary of the Royal Society', which is doubtful. The question does not use it.
